Hi Cristine, (cc list)

I just tried it in Distance 6.0 release 2 and it worked fine for me.

Check under File | Project Properties | Geographic that the Geographic=20
coordinate system is none and the shapefile units are meters.  You might=20
get the behaviour you describe if Distance thinks you're entering lat=20
and long coordinates.

Another potential problem might arise if you use a comma "," instead of=20
period "." to denote the decimal in your region.  If your Windows=20
settings are such that it's expecting a "," then you'd need to enter
452564,0347 5334957,719

If neither of these work, send me a copy of your project (use File |=20
Export project... and save as type zip) and I'll see if I can see what=20
the problem is by looking at it.

Cheers - Len

Thanks Eric!  I have decided to try out a Systematic Grid for the count
points and simply transit between them as though doing parallel
transects.

But I am now having difficulties with setting up a design with different
effort in different strata.  I have imported a shapefile for my overall
study area and checked that the map looks right.  I then imported
another shapefile as a stratum layer under the global parent layer, and
again the map for that looks right. When I come to the Design Properties
box I can chose my stratum layer but when I go to the Effort Allocation
Tab and uncheck the 'Same effort for all strata' box, the list of my
different strata does NOT appear. If I go ahead as if it is a single
strata, then I get this message:=20

Source:D5DesPrp.PointSamplerProperties.CreateListFromFlexGrid
Internal Error number: 9
Internal Error description: "Subscript out of range"

In fact, sometimes it doesn't let me get to the Effort Allocation tab at
all and says 'An unexpected error occurred while checking the options on
this page. Please check they are valid and change any incorrect values'.

Both my shapefiles are projected as BNG and I've had no problems with
doing a design for my 'global' shapefile. Is there something I need to
do with my strata shapefile for the different polygons to be recognised?

Thanks
Linda

Distance survey design engine (systematic grid sampling) to place a set=20=

of systematic points into your study area, then after that=20design is=20

messages.subject: Planning long term wildlife monitoring
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I am planning a study in which we will apply the Density Surface Modellin=
g tool in Distance 6.0 to estimate the abundance of, and identify "hotspo=

ts" of, marine wildlife in northwestern Australia.

The programme is aimed to span the next four years (and will possibly be =
continued afterwards provided sufficient funding comes through). Our curr=
ent budget and other logistical constraints however only allow us to cove=
r the area during three consecutive months each year.=20

Ideally, we would be interested in getting a "seasonal picture" of marine=
 mammal occurrence but we would also like to qualify the status of certai=
n populations of interest (decreasing, stable, increasing) by conducting =

trends/time series analyses.

We are thinking of two possible sampling plans:

1) Choosing an invariant three-month period and sampling the area repeate=
dly every year at this time - thereby enhancing our sample size for these=
 particular months (and possibly the robustness of trend analyses ?), yet=

 at the loss of an understanding of seasonal variations in abundance.

messages.body_plain:
Phil:

You ask an interesting question.  It is independent of distance sampling
and density surface modelling, but is something that almost everybody
conducting population assessment grapples with.

You will struggle to be able to say profound things about trends in
abundance with four years of data; folks with 40 years of data are
better equipped to address issues of trend.  Using the rotating panel
idea you'll be partially confounding year and season effects which will
also make interpretation of your findings a challenge.

There is a large and growing literature on the topic of your email; you
might excavate Len Steve and Ken's chapter on trend analysis in the
Advanced Distance Sampling book from 2004 for an entry point into this
literature.  Perhaps others on the list will offer an opinion, but I
don't think there are simple answers to your question.

messages.body_plain:
Distance Sampling members,

I used distance sampling to estimate deer density in the Black Hills of S=
outh Dakota. We conducted spotlight surveys between 10 August to 21 Augus=
t 2009. Roads were selected to represent habitat in proportion seen throu=
ghout the study area. The survey route consisted of 43.9 km on 8 transect=
s  that traveled through pine forest, meadows, aspen, and spruce. Deer we=
re counted on the same route 8 different nights. Two trucks ran 4 transec=
ts each night and switched routes every other night. We hypothesized that=
 due to terrain and sapling regeneration along roads observers from the b=
ack of the vehicle would detect more animals because of a better angle an=
d higher view. We used 4 observers with 2 positioned in the cab and 2 obs=
ervers in the back of the truck.  The front was considered the primary ob=
server and the back counted any additional animals the front did not see.=
  The observers switched roles at the beginning of each new transect to e=
nsure that sightability differences were caused by position in the vehicl=
e and not the observer.  We assumed that sighting probabilities associate=
d with each observer did not change with their role as primary or seconda=
ry observer. An observer could signal that a deer had been seen, but the =
count of each deer group was not announced until the vehicle had passed t=
he deer group.=20

Only one distance was recorded for each group sighting, so basically I wa=
s looking at the difference in total counts between front and back of the=
 truck.

I am struggling with how I should analyze this data in distance?  Should =
I use a double-observer technique in the MCDS engine?  Or do I have to us=
e MRDS. I am afraid that observer independence assumption would be violat=
ed if using the MRDS engine.  I thought maybe another option would be to =
develop a correction factor for total count and add that as a multiplier =
in the CDS engine.

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.
Thanks for your time,

messages.body_plain:
Angela:

The analysis of anyone's data ought to be driven by the design of the=20
data collection.  In your situation, what was the motivation for having=20
two sets of observers if they were not operating independently, or=20
setting up trials for one another?  Further, why would you place the=20
'primary' data gatherers in the least optimal viewing locations?

Were you trying to overcome failure to detect deer on the trackline (the =

g(0) problem); in which you use the independent observer method=20
accounting for duplicate detections.  Did you fear there was responsive=20
movement on the part of the deer to your approach (in which case you=20
should have used the Buckland-Turnock configuration) where one observer=20
was setting up trials for the other observer (but this relies upon a=20
particular type of viewing behaviour on the part of the tracker (in the=20
back of the truck) and the ability to determine successes/failures of=20
observers in the cab).

If you were simply trying to get lots of eyeballs looking for deer, then =

you really were not employing a double observer protocol per se, such=20
that the MRDS analytical protocol does not apply.

Prof. Buckland would find me remiss if I did not also mention that your=20
use of roads results in non-random sampling of the area you are trying=20
to study, so your density estimates may well not be representative of=20
your study area, but rather the portion of your study area that is near=20
roads.  Similarly, it is likely the case that deer are not distributed=20
uniformly between the trackline out to your truncation distance (there=20
is little for a deer to eat in the centre of a gravel road so deer are=20
unlikely to be there, if sapling regeneration is good all the road edges =

there are more likely to be there browsing).  See the forthcoming paper=20
*Point Transect Sampling Along Linear Features, *T. A. Marques, S. T.=20
Buckland, D. L. Borchers, D. Tosh, R. A. McDonald DOI:=20
10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x appearing soon in Biometrics for a=20
discussion of this non-uniform distribution issue.

So you have a handful of sampling issues you need to ponder beyond your=20
multiple observer matter.

case, but hard for me to evaluate.
